name: Ocean
lede: Ocean is a deep blue-green, the color the word suggests today; for most of European history, though, water was painted green, and the sea took a long time to become blue.

sections.title: The swatch and the word
sections.body:
The swatch is #017B92, a blue-green slightly greener than [[cerulean]], which is its nearest named color in the app palette at a distance of 7.4 CIEDE2000 units [1]. Our library takes the name from the xkcd color-name list, and the earliest record of it in our sources is 2010, so as a modern screen color it is young [1]. Its closest relatives are [[sea-blue]], [[ocean-blue]] and [[teal-blue]], with [[sea]] and [[turquoise]] a little greener [1].

An older dictionary use points the other way. Paterson lists *ocean green* as a yellowy green, which is a different color from our blue-green swatch [2]. The word has meant both, and the swatch should not be read back into older texts [2].

sections.title: When the sea was green
sections.body:
Water was rarely thought of as blue in ancient and medieval societies, Pastoureau writes [3]. In pictures it could be any color, but symbolically it was mostly tied to green [3]. On the oldest maps, oceans, lakes and rivers were almost always green, and the shift to blue began only in the late fifteenth century [3]. He adds that seas and oceans passed from green to blue very slowly, between the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries [4]. In everyday imagination it took longer still [3].

Pastoureau suggests that the growing link between blue and water probably played the largest part in blue changing from a warm color to a cool one [3].

sections.title: Homer's wine-dark sea
sections.body:
The best-known ancient sea color is Homer's *oinops*, usually rendered wine-dark [5][6]. Ball cites the suggestion that Greek color words described lustre and brightness at least as much as hue: the same word is used in Greek literature for darkened blood and for a cloud, or for the glint of metal and for a tree [5]. Paterson's dictionary reads it the same way, as a sign that the Greeks cared more about the brightness of a surface than its hue [6].

In 1858 the statesman Gladstone counted color words in Homer and found black the most frequent, with about 170 mentions, and blue not mentioned once [7]. The claim that the Greeks could not see blue is a myth, and the counts do not prove it: Gage points out that blue pigments, bright and saturated ones made from Egyptian blue, were in use from Mycenaean to Hellenistic times [8]. What the counts show is how few color terms Homer used and how he used them, not what the eye could see [5][8].

sections.title: Why deep water looks blue-green
sections.body:
Gurney's painters' rule is that the sea tends to blue-green, because those wavelengths survive the longest passage through water [9]. Westland gives two reasons for blue water, that it reflects the sky and that its longer wavelengths are absorbed more strongly than short ones [10]. The two books stress different causes, so the sky's part is a matter of emphasis.

The angle matters too. Looking steeply down into a lake or ocean from a boat, Gurney notes, little light from the sky reaches the eye and the water looks dark [11]. At shallow angles the surface reflects more, and a reflected light object appears slightly darker than the object itself, because some light enters the water instead [11].

sections.title: Ocean in other words
sections.body:
The sea has lent its name to colors that have nothing to do with its hue. *Ultramarine* means beyond the sea: Finlay explains that medieval Italians used *oltramarino* as a technical term for imported goods, and the paint came from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan [12]. The Indian Ocean mattered for another blue: Balfour-Paul writes that sailors and merchants carried indigo and dyed textiles along its routes [13].

The ocean also became a figure for color itself. Pastoureau notes that Charles Le Brun, defending drawing, compared color to an ocean where many drown [14]. And one film legend ties the word to a stone: Finlay reports that, according to film lore, James Cameron chose [[gem:tanzanite|tanzanite]] for the jewel in *Titanic* because blue diamonds looked too dark to him and sapphires too dull [15]. Treat that as lore, since the book itself flags it so [15].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Ocean is rare in painting. In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, only 9 have a patch within six units of this color (CIEDE2000) covering at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [16]. Where it appears, it is usually a mid-tone (89 per cent of the matches), not a shadow or a highlight [16].

None of the six strongest matches is a seascape. They include [[painting:nga-56746|Sisters in Blue]] (1840), where it covers 31 per cent of the canvas, [[painting:aic-109780|Love of Winter]] (1914), and [[painting:nga-46657|Palazzo da Mula, Venice]] by [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] (1908) [16]. The match is concentrated in the 1900s, with 3 of 1,674 paintings, and in Impressionism, with 1 of 140 [16]. The earliest match, a portrait of 1510, is a look-alike hue and not evidence of any pigment [16]. In printed English the word *ocean* peaks about 1978, but it counts the water itself, so it says nothing about the color [16].

These numbers are for museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [16].
